claims.claim_text: Altium descends from Protel, written in Borland Turbo Pascal as a DOS PCB editor by Nick Martin at the University of Tasmania in 1985; the companion schematic tool followed two to three years later, and a lower-cost edition, Easy Tracks, shipped with a hardware dongle.
claims.quote_verbatim: he wrote the DOS-based PCB tool. It was called Protel PCB back then
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Protel for Windows, released in the early 1990s, was among the first PCB tools written for Windows, at a time when it was not settled whether Windows or the Mac OS would become the dominant desktop platform.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the first PCB tool by donkey's years for Windows
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Protel 99 SE, released around the company's 1999 stock-market listing, remained an industry standard for roughly twenty years and was used by practically every development house in China.
claims.quote_verbatim: which was the industry standard tool for 20 years
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A long-lived design tool accumulates a stable set of known defects; an experienced designer catalogues them and routes around them rather than waiting for fixes. Twelve documented defects in Protel 99 SE were handled this way.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know how to just avoid the bugs happening
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The rename from Protel to Altium in the early 2000s resolved internal competition between the PCAD and Protel product lines, which were sold at similar price points to overlapping users; PCAD's strength was PCB and Protel's was schematic, and the two were hybridised into Altium Designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: to sell two products within the same company at a similar price point to user bases that loved both meant that we were competing with ourselves internally
claims.speaker: Matt Berggren

claims.claim_text: In an overnight repricing announced to staff by founder Nick Martin, the package was cut roughly 80 percent, from around eight to ten thousand dollars to a flat two thousand dollars, framed internally as irreversible. Customers who had recently paid the old price were left holding it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we are burning our bridges. We can't go back to high price software
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: After its stock-market listing the company redirected its product strategy around FPGAs on the premise that FPGAs would displace microcontrollers, a decision driven personally by the founder in a flat organisation where nothing proceeded without his approval.
claims.quote_verbatim: Nick decided that, oh, yeah, we're going all FPGA
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The NanoBoard NB2, a four-thousand-dollar FPGA development board bundled with a licence that deliberately excluded the PCB tool, was built on the premise that customers would assemble products from prebuilt modules and never lay out a custom board again. It did not sell and distributor stock was returned; the successor NanoBoard 3000 was priced an order of magnitude lower at around three hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: It priced itself out of the market
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The FPGA tooling let a designer drag in vendor-portable blocks including processor cores, and included C-to-HDL synthesis, so a simple application could be built without writing Verilog or VHDL. It worked well at that level of abstraction and obstructed work on serious projects that needed access to the underlying detail.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could even do it like from schematics
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Founder Nick Martin was removed by the board in 2012 while remaining the company's largest single shareholder with roughly a quarter of its stock, after a decade in which the company had repeatedly taken losses on ventures outside its core PCB and schematic product line.
claims.quote_verbatim: He was just booted out by the board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: A design-tool vendor's country of R&D is a procurement constraint for defence customers: after the company relocated its headquarters and R&D to China it was reported to be losing United States military-sector business under rules governing dealings with companies based there.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are rules and regulations in the U.S. about how you can deal and what products you can get from a company that is effectively based in China
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: The company relocated its base repeatedly: to San Jose in the 1990s and back to Sydney, to China around 2012, and to San Diego in 2014, with a substantial share of development carried out in Ukraine after the China move.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the 90s, Altium packed up and moved to San Jose in the US
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Renesas acquired Altium at sixty-eight Australian dollars a share, roughly a third above the prevailing market price and about twenty-four times revenue, in the largest Japanese acquisition of an Australian-listed company. The company was debt-free and, despite a United States headquarters, remained Australian-registered.
claims.quote_verbatim: the largest acquisition of any company on the Australian stock exchange by a Japanese firm in history
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium owns Octopart, one of the two major cross-distributor part search engines alongside FindChips, giving the vendor a pricing and availability data source inside its own tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium own Octopart. They bought that quite a long time ago
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Octopart and Ciiva were acquired to serve as the component database and library back end for CircuitMaker, with the same infrastructure intended to feed Altium Designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: Octopart and SIVA are the back end
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: List pricing has moved by large multiples over time: a roughly seventy percent cut from about twelve thousand dollars to three or four thousand in the early 2010s, and a return to eight to ten thousand dollars in the United States within a few years.
claims.quote_verbatim: at that time, Altium was quite cheap
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Reported pricing settled around five thousand dollars for an initial seat with fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars a year for maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: 5,000 the first time, 2,000 a year after that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Altium does not publish its pricing; figures circulating among users were around six thousand dollars a seat with about twenty-five hundred a year for maintenance, and letting maintenance lapse stops the tool working under the newer terms.
claims.quote_verbatim: 6K for a seat and about 2,500 for maintenance
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The list price is negotiable and varies with the sales cycle; approaching a representative near the end of a quota period improves the outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium price famously varies depending on how actual loudly you shout at them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A practical negotiating method for expensive design-tool seats is to name a price to the representative, stay civil, and be willing to wait a year rather than close: representatives hold latitude and will come back if they can meet the number.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to be willing to walk away
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: A perpetual licence is a requirement in the professional ECAD market rather than a preference, because a design that has been released must remain openable in the tool version that produced it.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the professional market for ECAD software, you have to offer a perpetual license
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Archiving the tool alongside the design at each release is sound engineering practice, and is only possible where a perpetual licence exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: they back up their tools with their design, that's good design
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Under perpetual licensing the burden falls on the vendor to justify each upgrade, and the user can decline a direction they dislike by staying on the version they own; under subscription the same user has no lever and absorbs each change.
claims.quote_verbatim: you simply don't buy the next version
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium withdrew the perpetual licence in favour of term-based licensing, which users reported as roughly doubling the annualised cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're getting rid of perpetual, and it's only term-based licenses
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Later pricing restructured around a shared workspace with author seats at thirteen hundred dollars a year plus collaborator seats, spreading licence cost across everyone in the value chain who touches the design rather than concentrating it on the layout engineer.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium Designer, Authors. $1,300 a year
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Committing to a PCB package is effectively a ten-year decision because the accumulated design corpus is locked into that tool's format, and vendors price and negotiate in the knowledge that the transaction cost of leaving is high.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're not going to change that for 10 years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Arduino, IndiGoGo and Hack-a-Day - Doodad Dealer Dancing

claims.claim_text: Inside established companies nobody is rewarded for evaluating tools, so a better tool does not displace an incumbent on merit; the investment already sunk into the incumbent decides the outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: the switching costs are very high
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: One shop's tool history ran from HighWire through DipTrace and Eagle to Altium; the move came when Eagle went to online subscription and Altium halved its price to capture the displaced users. A competitor's licensing change, not a feature comparison, was the trigger.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium came around to everybody and they cut the price of Altium basically in half
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: Altium's licence enforcement watches the client address; a shop whose internet connection presents several rotating IP addresses triggers licence-compliance contact from the vendor, which is a practical constraint on network design at the customer site.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a number of IP addresses and when they see it bounce around
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: Altium has supplied university licences for decades, so graduates arrive trained on it. For a small employer that does not hold a seat, this converts into a hiring cost: either buy another expensive seat or retrain the new engineer onto the tool the company owns.
claims.quote_verbatim: I hire someone. I can't afford another Altium license
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: The licence cost puts the tool out of reach of an engineer without an employer, which makes capable open-source packages an accessibility requirement rather than a preference.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I didn't work at a company, I probably wouldn't be able to afford to buy it
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar

claims.claim_text: Board complexity, not professional status, is the test for whether the expense is justified; designs at the size and complexity of a Raspberry Pi do not require it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It comes down to what boards you're doing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The professional PCB tool market segments by company size and age: long-established larger firms run Cadence, while Altium holds the small and medium segment.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium really has that, that small and medium size company segment
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Export analytics from a cross-tool component library service put Altium at roughly thirty percent of downloads, Eagle at about twenty-five percent, and KiCad, OrCAD and Allegro at roughly fifteen percent each.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium is probably like 30%
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: The intended method treats the schematic as the control document: part numbers, supplier data and fit/no-fit attributes all live in the schematic and are pushed forward to generate bills of materials in whatever templates are needed. Adopting the method partially yields none of its benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you commit 100% to do it that way, it doesn't work
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Altium and KiCad place only the schematic symbol at capture time and defer footprint assignment to layout, whereas Eagle binds a package to each device variant in the library. The consequence is that the designer, not the library, owns footprint correctness, and unprepared footprints turn a layout task into library work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're the librarian at that point with those kinds of tools
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Professional-tier tools assume a librarian produces correct part data before schematic capture begins, so the work of getting symbols and footprints in order is front-loaded and typically consumes weeks before layout starts.
claims.quote_verbatim: they require you to kind of get everything correct up front
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Altium supports several incompatible approaches to library management and never settled on one, leaving each group to choose a method and enforce it internally.
claims.quote_verbatim: there were multiple ways to do libraries
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Generating library parts once in a neutral format and exporting per tool works for symbols and ordinary pads, but breaks down on features the tools represent differently. Slotted holes are the hard case: Eagle requires the milling layer, some tools have no slotted-hole primitive at all, and KiCad only gained the shape relatively recently.
claims.quote_verbatim: Slotted holes in particular are quite challenging
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Maintaining a mechanically accurate library was a staffed function inside Altium, with mechanical engineers and dedicated library staff producing precise 3D models for every part so designers could request a model and receive it within the hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: all our parts had to be precisely 3d modeled
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The tool includes an IPC footprint generator: the dimensions from the data sheet are entered and the footprint is produced to IPC standards, rather than being drawn by hand or taken from a vendor library.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium designer actually has an IPC footprint generator
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An individual placed instance can have its pads edited without changing the library component. This is fast for prototyping, when a nearly-correct footprint needs a slightly larger hole or pad, and it is dangerous because it silently breaks the correspondence between the known-good library footprint and what is fabricated.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually edit the pads of each individual component as needed without having to edit the library component
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: An OutJob is a scripted output definition; a company-standard OutJob produces an identical set of manufacturing files across every project regardless of who ran it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it generates exactly the same format files every time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because output generation is scripted, a misconfigured OutJob fails silently. In one case a four-layer board was exported with only two layers and the fault was found only after the fabricator's upload preview disagreed with the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: he was only outputting, exporting two layers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium treats plane layers differently from signal layers and emits inner planes as negative images, which some fabricators will not render or accept. The workaround is to build inner planes as flood-filled signal layers instead, which produces positive artwork and avoids the problem entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: JLC PCB doesn't like the inverse inner copper layers that Altium produces
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: KiCad emits positive artwork even for plane layers, so a four-layer board exported from it does not raise the negative-plane issue at the fabricator.
claims.quote_verbatim: it generates positive, uh, images, right? Even for planes
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium's conception of a board outline layer differs from that of other tools and the outline is typically not contiguous, which fabricators have to accommodate on the receiving end.
claims.quote_verbatim: their outline layers are actually typically not actually contiguous
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Fabricator upload tools recognise Altium's Gerber file-extension convention, such as .gbl for bottom copper, and assign layers automatically from the file names.
claims.quote_verbatim: it obviously knows the Altium layer naming format
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Two panelisation methods are available and they trade differently. The built-in tool copies the source board file so every layer is duplicated faithfully; manual copy-and-paste panelisation also works but risks omitting a selection, and design-rule checking a hand-built panel is much harder, so it demands manual verification or a check at the Gerber stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing a DRC on a panel is much more difficult
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Release was structured as a procedure rather than a habit: run the design rule check, generate the Gerbers and the bill of materials, then check the design in.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do your DRC, you generate your Gerbers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Silkscreen bitmap import is not a built-in feature but a long-lived community script, which is representative of how much of the tool's peripheral functionality is delivered: the documented method is to run a script.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium's very script based
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: The design rule system distinguishes via-level clearance from track-level clearance, which is what allows a dense board to be routed without relaxing the track rules globally.
claims.quote_verbatim: is there a via level clearance versus just a track level clearance? Yes, there is
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Before automatic length matching existed, matched-length routing was done by reading the reported trace length and manually shuffling segments to add or remove the needed distance.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could tell you the length of the trace
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: On the author's first HDI designs, the 3D stack-up visualisation was used heavily to reason about layer transitions; the need for it falls away once the designer has built an internal model of the stack, so the feature matters most during the transition into high-density work.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you have developed a kind of intuition for this 3D visualization
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: The enclosure model can be imported and the board inserted into it, and the tool runs a design rule check on the mechanical fit, highlighting a connector that does not line up with its panel cutout.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure all the connectors fit the cutouts on the front panel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: AD620, DesignSpark, Instrumentation Amplifier - The Rant Rhetorical

claims.claim_text: Scripting against the tool's bill of materials data allows the whole procurement step to be automated: quantities in, current vendor pricing pulled, purchase orders emitted in each vendor's required template. Run at design time, the same pipeline turns a component substitution into an immediate readout of manufacturing cost and lead time.
claims.quote_verbatim: it automatically gets all the latest prices from all the different vendors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Schematic and PCB differencing is built into the tool and highlights what changed, which is the capability version control of hardware designs depends on; where it is absent, revision control of a design is impractical.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium have their own built-in diff things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: Files written by a newer version can be opened in an older one, a property the vendor maintained for decades and which professional users treat as essential.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could even load a, like a version 20 file into a version 16
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: On the Steam Controller programme the CAD version was frozen at Altium 12 for the duration, importing a semiconductor-industry practice of locking tool and design-rule versions across a long project so that a defect in the CAD cannot disrupt the schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to settle on Altium 12 for
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The interface overhaul between versions 16 and 19 removed menu items and reorganised the interaction model, returning an expert user to being slow and ineffective. Reaching genuine proficiency takes about a year of intensive use, so an interface change of that size is a schedule cost to every established user, not a preference question.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are a few things that are more soul crushing and kind of humiliating than being an expert in a tool
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Falling back to an older version as a crutch after an interface change is a decaying strategy: supplier search and manufacturing-parameter features in old versions stop working as distributors change their APIs, and those versions do not receive the updates.
claims.quote_verbatim: DigiKey and others change their APIs
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: SolidWorks holds its interaction model stable across releases; the argument drawn from the contrast is that a professional design tool should either preserve its interface or allow the old one to be restored, because a designer earning a living in the tool cannot absorb months of reduced effectiveness.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fundamental way that you interact with SolidWorks has not really changed in a very, very long time
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Sales experience inverted the expected difficulty: converting a user from a competing package was easier than persuading an existing user to move to the next version, because the incumbent version's bugs and quirks were already known and worked around.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was easier to get people to change to Altium than it was to get people to upgrade to the next version of Altium
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The in-house hardware group was required to design real products on the latest daily build, so that user-facing defects were found by engineers doing production work rather than by customers.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to design our own boards using not just Altium, but the latest daily build every day
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Designing production work on daily builds did occasionally corrupt the file format mid-project, but because the developers were in the same building they wrote conversion scripts on request and no work was lost. The practice is only survivable where that recovery path exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: we accidentally corrupted the file format
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: The design file format is binary and undocumented, so importers in other tools are written against reverse-engineered structure and cannot be relied upon.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Altium haven't published their binary
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Converting boards from Eagle into Altium produced poor results, and the damage persists beyond the conversion because the imported library parts carry the defects forward: a component that arrives with twelve unnecessary layers puts those layers on every future board that uses it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pain stays with you
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The original CircuitMaker plan was a free base package with capabilities bought as needed, on the order of fifty dollars to unlock eight layers for a month. The product shipped instead as entirely free with no feature limits.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be a basic free package. And then you buy all these add-ons
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: CircuitMaker's free terms required published projects, but a project stays private until it is committed and a local copy is held on disk, so the publication requirement applies at commit rather than at every edit.
claims.quote_verbatim: As long as you don't commit the project, it stays private and a local copy is actually stored on your hard drive
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: CircuitMaker was deliberately degraded with a random sleep so that it would not compete with the paid product. The vendor's public account attributed slowdowns to designs above roughly five thousand connections; users reported the degradation regardless of size, along with parts disappearing or relocating during drag operations that were side effects of the deliberate routine rather than ordinary defects.
claims.quote_verbatim: a random sleep timer
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Upverter was acquired and made free, and CircuitMaker was folded into it as Upverter Desktop, the offline-capable counterpart to the browser-based Upverter Online.
claims.quote_verbatim: It will be renamed up. Upverter desktop
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Circuit Studio was made deliberately file-incompatible with Altium Designer so that a company could not buy a small number of full seats and staff the rest of the work on cheap ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: They want to make it as hard as possible
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Circuit Studio launched at three to four thousand dollars, a price point between the free and professional tiers that attracted neither, and was later cut to nine hundred and ninety-five dollars with a hundred and twenty-five dollar annual maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was the no man's land of CAD pricing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Circuit Studio was built at Element 14's request so the distributor would have its own higher-end tool to sell, distributed exclusively through it, and was then left without upgrades for around five years while paying customers continued to hold licences.
claims.quote_verbatim: the lights have been out on Circuit Studio for like five years now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium 365 is the vendor's cloud design-review and collaboration layer, and it stores designs in its own workspace rather than integrating with GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, which is the constraint for teams whose review process is already anchored on one of those.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is kind of their, their cloud, cloud-based, uh, um, design review system
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Altium 365 was positioned as shared, in-browser access to a design in the way a document is shared, and it brought that capability to mid-market teams for whom the previous route was a substantially more expensive enterprise licence.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was supposed to be like Google Docs for PCB design
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: The cloud layer was made optional rather than mandatory, so a shop that declines it keeps working locally, which is the distinction from competitors who removed the local-only path.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you do not want to participate in the cloud, you do not have to participate in the cloud
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The cloud platform allows a manufacturer to annotate a design in place with process-specific feedback, for example that a BGA sits close enough to a capacitor to cause thermal shadowing, turning fabrication review into feedback during layout rather than after release.
claims.quote_verbatim: a manufacturer could go in and, and push manufacturing data into, into a design
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: SolidWorks PCB is a rebadged Altium product, so a shop nominally standardised on the SolidWorks ECAD tool is on the same underlying package.
claims.quote_verbatim: SolidWorks PCB. It's just Altium
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Circuit Studio originated as Element 14's high-end offering after Eagle became the distributor's low-end tool, and was priced around three thousand dollars at introduction.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they convinced Altium to, uh, yeah, make this Circuit Studio for them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: A consultancy that could reuse whole schematic blocks deliberately does not, reusing components but not blocks, because each application varies the input voltage and output current enough that copying carries a design across without its derivation. Traceability and design notes are the stated reason, and the practical reason templates never get built is that billable backlog crowds them out.
claims.quote_verbatim: even a buck converter, every application will use that buck converter slightly differently
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Reusable schematic blocks are a capability KiCad lacked and Altium supported, which is what makes block-level reuse a live design decision in one tool and not the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: a key cad is actually terrible at a reusable block
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Reusable blocks reached KiCad in its version 10 previews, closing that gap.
claims.quote_verbatim: reusable blocks is going to be in key CAD
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Sharing a complete project, schematic and layout together, through a browser link is used in consulting practice as evidence of prior work when winning a client, without requiring the client to hold a licence.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just need the web browser
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: Shipping a separate simplified product rather than a feature-limited build of the main one commits the vendor to maintaining two code bases, which is a permanent tax on engineering capacity.
claims.quote_verbatim: now they have to maintain two different programs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: The differentiation between the free and professional products was drawn on productivity rather than capability: the cheaper tool remains able to do the work but takes longer, so daily layout work justifies the paid seat on time alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will take out some of the things that make Altium Designer more productive
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Altium dominated Chinese board design for years largely through unlicensed copies, which is why files arriving from that supply chain are overwhelmingly in its format.
claims.quote_verbatim: they weren't paid for copies
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: On large designs the money buys automation and polish rather than capability that is otherwise unreachable; on smaller designs the same automation has little to act on, which is the shape of the buy-or-not decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're paying for a more polished, automated experience
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
